title: Concurrency basics
scopeHtml:
Scope: race conditions, critical sections, mutex, spinlock, semaphores, condition variables, atomics, memory ordering and spotting lock contention.

Scope: race conditions, critical sections, mutex, spinlock, semaphores, condition variables, atomics, memory ordering and spotting lock contention.

notes.title: Race conditions
notes.html:
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the exact timing of two threads. Two threads touch the same data, at least one writes, and nothing orders them. The program works 999,999 times and corrupts data on the millionth.

The classic: counter++ looks like one step but is three: load the value into a register, add 1, store it back. Two threads can both load 5, both add 1, both store 6. One increment is lost.

Thread A            Thread B            counter in memory
load  r1 = 5                            5
                    load  r2 = 5        5
add   r1 = 6                            5
                    add   r2 = 6        5
store counter = 6                       6
                    store counter = 6   6   <- should be 7

Worked example. Two threads each run counter++ 1,000,000 times with no protection. Expected 2,000,000. Typical result on a 4-core box: about 1.1 to 1.5 million, different every run. Under a debugger or with a printf added the bug often vanishes, because timing changes. That is the signature of a race: a "Heisenbug".

# Detect it: build with ThreadSanitizer and run
gcc -fsanitize=thread -g race.c -o race -lpthread && ./race
# WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=4121)
#   Write of size 4 at 0x... by thread T2:
#     #0 worker race.c:9
#   Previous write of size 4 at 0x... by thread T1:
#     #0 worker race.c:9

A data race (formal: unsynchronised conflicting accesses) is not the same as a race condition (a logic bug depending on ordering). You can have a race condition with no data race: two threads each take a lock correctly, but "check balance then withdraw" is done in two separate locked steps, so both pass the check.

Industry examples. The Therac-25 radiation overdoses (1980s) involved a race in the operator-input code. The 2003 US Northeast blackout was partly blamed on a race in an alarm system (GE XA/21). Java's HashMap used from many threads has been known to loop forever in get under concurrent resize (pre-Java 8). Go ships a built-in detector (go run -race) and many companies run it in CI.

Everyday analogy. Two people editing the same paper form at once: both read "seats left: 5", both write "4", and the airline sells 6 tickets for 5 seats.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing counter++ is atomic because it is one line of code. It is not, even in C, Java or Kotlin.
  • Confusing data race with race condition. Name both; give the check-then-act example for the second.
  • Saying "volatile fixes it". volatile gives visibility, not atomic read-modify-write.

notes.title: Critical sections
notes.html:
A critical section is the piece of code that touches shared data and must run by only one thread at a time. Everything else the thread does can run in parallel. The goal is to make critical sections as small as possible, because while one thread is inside, all others wait.

A correct solution to mutual exclusion needs three properties:

  1. Mutual exclusion: at most one thread inside.
  2. Progress: if the section is free and someone wants in, someone gets in; no deadlock from the protocol itself.
  3. Bounded waiting: no thread waits forever (no starvation).

Worked example. A request handler spends 50 microseconds parsing (parallel), then 5 microseconds updating a shared stats table (critical), then 200 microseconds writing the response (parallel). Only 5 of 255 microseconds are serialised. By Amdahl's law, the maximum speed-up is 1 / serial fraction = 255 / 5 = 51x. If you wrongly hold the lock during the response write, the serial part is 205 of 255, and the cap drops to about 1.2x. Adding cores then does nothing.

Decision gravity. Lock granularity: one global lock (simple, no deadlocks, poor scaling), per-object locks (scales, deadlock risk), lock-free structures (best scaling, very hard to get right). Start coarse; refine only when profiling shows lock contention. It is reversible if the lock is hidden behind a small class; a one-way door if callers are expected to hold your lock.

Industry examples. The old Linux "Big Kernel Lock" (BKL) was one global lock; it took years (removed fully in 2.6.39) to split into fine-grained locks. CPython's GIL is the same trade: a single global lock makes the interpreter simple and single-thread fast but caps CPU-bound threads at about one core.

Everyday analogy. A single-stall toilet: everyone does other things in parallel, but only one person can be inside, and a long stay hurts everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • Doing I/O or calling unknown code (callbacks) while holding a lock: long hold times and hidden deadlocks.
  • Forgetting that reads need protection too if writers exist.
  • Not naming the three properties (exclusion, progress, bounded waiting).

notes.title: Mutex
notes.html:
A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) lets one thread own a critical section; others sleep until it is released. Operations: lock and unlock. The key point is that a waiting thread is put to sleep by the kernel, so it burns no CPU.

How Linux implements it (the futex, fast userspace mutex): the lock is one integer in user memory.

  • Uncontended lock: one atomic compare-and-swap from 0 to 1 in user space. No syscall. About 20 ns.
  • Contended lock: the thread calls the futex(FUTEX_WAIT) syscall and the kernel parks it. unlock sees waiters and calls futex(FUTEX_WAKE). A contended lock costs a syscall plus a context switch, about 2 to 10 microseconds.
# See it live: threads stuck on a mutex show as futex waits
strace -f -c -p 2310
# % time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
#  91.40    4.812211        1203      4000       812 futex
// Java: synchronized or ReentrantLock (both are mutexes with sleeping waiters)
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
void withdraw(long amt) {
    lock.lock();
    try { if (balance >= amt) balance -= amt; }
    finally { lock.unlock(); }     // always unlock in finally
}

Properties to know: a mutex has an owner (only the locker may unlock). Recursive (reentrant) mutexes let the same thread lock again; Java synchronized and ReentrantLock are reentrant, a default pthread_mutex_t is not (relocking self-deadlocks). Priority inversion: a low-priority thread holds the lock, a high-priority one waits, a medium-priority thread keeps the CPU. The 1997 Mars Pathfinder kept resetting because of exactly this; the fix was enabling priority inheritance on the mutex (PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT).

Industry examples. Go's sync.Mutex has a normal mode and a "starvation mode" (after a waiter fails 1 ms, ownership is handed over directly). Java's synchronized starts as a cheap biased/thin lock and inflates to an OS-backed monitor under contention (biased locking was removed in JDK 18+).

Everyday analogy. A key to a single meeting room: take the key, use the room, hang the key back. If the key is gone you wait on the sofa (sleep), not by pounding on the door.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to unlock on an exception path. Use try/finally, RAII (std::lock_guard) or defer mu.Unlock().
  • Locking different locks for the same data in different code paths.
  • Thinking a mutex is free. Contended mutexes with many threads show up as futex time in strace and high context-switch rate in vmstat.

notes.title: Spinlock
notes.html:
A spinlock makes a waiting thread loop on the CPU until the lock frees, instead of sleeping. It wastes cycles while waiting but avoids the cost of a context switch, so it wins only when the lock is held for a very short time (less than the cost of sleeping, roughly under 1 to 2 microseconds).

Minimal test-and-set spinlock:

lock:    while (atomic_exchange(&flag, 1) == 1) { pause; }   // spin
unlock:  atomic_store(&flag, 0)

The pause (x86) hint reduces power and helps the sibling hyper-thread. Better variants: test-and-test-and-set (spin on a plain read first so the cache line stays shared, then try the atomic), and ticket / MCS locks (each waiter spins on its own cache line, fair and no cache-line stampede).

Worked example. Critical section = 100 ns. Sleeping and waking costs about 5 microseconds of latency. A spinner waits about 100 ns; a sleeper waits 5,000 ns, 50 times longer. But if the holder is preempted by the scheduler while holding the lock (on a single core, or oversubscribed), spinners burn their whole time slice (say 4 ms) doing nothing. Rule: spinlocks are for kernels and for short, non-preemptible sections.

Industry examples. The Linux kernel uses spinlocks everywhere in interrupt context, where sleeping is forbidden: the holder disables preemption (and often local interrupts) with spin_lock_irqsave. Queued spinlocks (qspinlock, MCS-based) are the modern kernel default. Many user-space libraries (glibc adaptive mutex, Java's adaptive spinning in monitors) spin briefly and then sleep: the best of both.

Everyday analogy. Waiting at a lift with the door about to open: you stand and stare for two seconds. If the lift is stuck on floor 30, you would walk away and read a book (sleep).

Common interview traps.

  • Using a pure spinlock in user space on an oversubscribed machine (more threads than cores). Throughput collapses.
  • Sleeping (calling anything that blocks, such as malloc with page fault or printk to a slow console) while holding a kernel spinlock: deadlock or "scheduling while atomic" panic.
  • Saying spinlocks are "faster". They are faster only for very short holds.

notes.title: Semaphores
notes.html:
A semaphore is a counter with two operations: wait (P, decrement, sleep if it would go below zero) and signal (V, increment, wake a sleeper). Dijkstra invented it in 1965. Unlike a mutex it has no owner: thread A can signal what thread B waited on.

Two main uses:

  • Counting semaphore (permits): initial value N means N resources. A connection pool of 20 is a semaphore starting at 20.
  • Binary semaphore (0/1) used as a signal: thread B waits, thread A signals "data is ready". This is how you order events across threads, which a mutex cannot do cleanly.
// Limit concurrent calls to a flaky downstream service to 10
private final Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(10);
String call() throws InterruptedException {
    permits.acquire();               // blocks if 10 are already in flight
    try { return http.get(url); }
    finally { permits.release(); }
}

Worked example. Downstream handles 200 concurrent requests before latency explodes. Each of your 8 app servers gets a semaphore of 25 (8 x 25 = 200). Excess callers either queue (bounded) or fail fast. This is the bulkhead pattern; Netflix Hystrix and Resilience4j implement it with semaphores or thread pools.

Linux has POSIX semaphores (sem_wait, sem_post, built on futexes) and System V semaphores (older, kernel objects, still seen in PostgreSQL's shared memory setup).

Decision gravity. Mutex vs binary semaphore: use a mutex for protecting data (ownership, priority inheritance, clear intent), a semaphore for counting resources or signalling. Reversible; mistakes show up as lost wake-ups or leaked permits.

Everyday analogy. A car park with 50 tickets: each car takes a ticket on entry and returns it on exit. At zero tickets the barrier stays shut.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a binary semaphore as a mutex and then releasing from the wrong place (no owner means no safety net).
  • Leaking permits on exceptions; always release in finally.
  • Not knowing semaphores can be initialised to 0 to mean "wait for an event".

notes.title: Condition variables
notes.html:
A condition variable lets a thread sleep until some condition on shared data becomes true. It always works together with a mutex that protects that data. Without it you either spin ("is it ready yet?") or sleep for a fixed time and waste latency.

Protocol (the pattern must be exactly this):

consumer:                          producer:
  lock(m)                            lock(m)
  while (queue is empty)             queue.push(item)
      wait(cv, m)   // atomically    signal(cv)
  item = queue.pop() // unlock+sleep unlock(m)
  unlock(m)

wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then reacquires the mutex before returning. The while loop (not if) is mandatory for two reasons: spurious wake-ups (the OS may wake a waiter for no reason) and stolen wake-ups (another consumer got the item first between the signal and your reacquire).

final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();
Item take() throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        while (queue.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await();   // loop, not if
        return queue.poll();
    } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}

Signal vs broadcast. signal wakes one waiter, broadcast (notifyAll) wakes all. Use broadcast when waiters wait for different conditions on the same cv, or when unsure; it costs a "thundering herd" of wake-ups. Linux futex has FUTEX_REQUEUE so glibc can move waiters from the cv to the mutex without waking them all at once.

Industry examples. Java's BlockingQueue, Go's sync.Cond, Kotlin channels (under the hood coroutines park instead of sleeping a thread) are all this pattern. Android's Handler/Looper message queue blocks in epoll (native) until a message arrives.

Everyday analogy. A bakery pager: you leave your lock-box key at the counter, go to sit down, and the buzzer wakes you; you walk back, retake your place and check your order is actually there.

Common interview traps.

  • if instead of while around wait: the classic bug.
  • Signalling without holding the mutex or without changing the condition under it: a lost wake-up (signal fires before the waiter sleeps, nobody ever wakes it).
  • Using wait on a cv with a different mutex than the one protecting the state.

notes.title: Atomics
notes.html:
An atomic operation is a read-modify-write that the hardware guarantees cannot be interrupted or interleaved with other cores' accesses to that location. On x86 it uses the lock prefix (lock xadd, lock cmpxchg), which locks the cache line for the instruction. On ARM it uses load-linked/store-conditional pairs (ldaxr/stlxr) or newer LSE instructions.

Key operations: fetch_add, exchange, and compare-and-swap (CAS): "set to new only if currently equal to expected; tell me if it worked". CAS is the building block for lock-free code:

AtomicLong counter = new AtomicLong();
counter.incrementAndGet();                 // lock xadd, no mutex

// Lock-free "update max" using a CAS loop
void recordMax(AtomicLong max, long v) {
    long cur;
    while (v > (cur = max.get()) && !max.compareAndSet(cur, v)) { /* retry */ }
}

Worked example. 8 threads incrementing one counter 10 million times each. With a mutex: about 1.5 to 3 seconds (contention, sleeping). With an atomic: about 0.5 to 1 second, because all 8 cores fight for one cache line. With a sharded counter (each thread increments its own padded slot, sum on read): about 0.03 seconds. Java's LongAdder does exactly this. Atomics remove sleeping but not cache-line bouncing; at hot spots you must shard.

ABA problem. CAS checks only the value. Thread 1 reads A, is paused; thread 2 changes A to B and back to A (maybe a freed and reused node); thread 1's CAS succeeds although the structure changed. Fixes: version-tagged pointers (AtomicStampedReference), hazard pointers, epoch reclamation (RCU in the Linux kernel).

Decision gravity. Atomics are right for counters, flags, reference swaps. For multi-field invariants (balance and history together) use a lock; lock-free algorithms for those are research-grade bugs waiting to happen. Reversible if hidden behind a class.

Industry examples. Linux uses atomic_t and refcount_t for reference counts; Netty and Kafka clients use atomics and CAS for state flags; Disruptor (LMAX) built a lock-free ring buffer doing millions of messages/s per core.

Everyday analogy. Writing on a whiteboard with a rule: "erase 5 and write 6 only if it still says 5, otherwise look again". No one can sneak in a different number mid-edit.

Common interview traps.

  • "Lock-free is always faster." Under heavy contention a CAS loop can retry endlessly (it is lock-free, not wait-free).
  • Ignoring false sharing: two unrelated atomics on the same 64-byte cache line slow each other. Pad to separate lines.
  • Using two atomics and assuming the pair is consistent.

notes.title: Memory ordering and visibility
notes.html:
Modern CPUs and compilers reorder memory operations and cache them per core, so one thread may see another's writes late or in a different order. Single-threaded code never notices, because the result looks the same. Across threads it matters.

Why it happens: compilers move and cache variables in registers; CPUs have store buffers (a write sits in a queue before reaching the cache) and out-of-order execution. x86 is strong (TSO: only a store followed by a load to a different address may reorder). ARM and POWER are weak (almost any reordering allowed), which is why code that "works on x86" breaks on Android phones and Apple silicon servers.

The classic broken pattern:

shared: int data = 0; bool ready = false;
Thread A:  data = 42;  ready = true;
Thread B:  while (!ready) {}  print(data);   // may print 0, or loop forever

Fix: use release/acquire pairs. A release store makes all earlier writes visible before the flag; an acquire load that sees the flag sees those writes.

volatile boolean ready;   // Java volatile = acquire on read, release on write (sequentially consistent)
int data;
// Thread A: data = 42; ready = true;
// Thread B: while (!ready) {} ; use(data);   // guaranteed to see 42

C++/Rust give explicit orders: relaxed (atomicity only), acquire, release, acq_rel, seq_cst (global order, the default and the safest). A memory barrier/fence instruction (mfence, dmb) enforces ordering. Mutex lock is an acquire and unlock a release, so data protected by a mutex needs no extra fences. This is the "happens-before" relation in the Java Memory Model.

Worked example: double-checked locking. The old Java singleton if (inst == null) { synchronized { if (inst == null) inst = new Foo(); } } was broken before Java 5: the reference could be published before the constructor finished, so another thread used a half-built object. Fix: declare inst volatile.

Decision gravity. Use seq_cst/volatile/mutexes by default. Weaker orderings give a few percent on hot paths and cost days of reasoning; choose them only with a benchmark and a tool such as ThreadSanitizer or a model checker (CDSChecker, Loom for Rust). Reversible at code level, but wrong code ships silently.

Industry examples. Linux kernel has a formal memory model (smp_mb(), READ_ONCE, WRITE_ONCE, smp_store_release). Java JMM (JSR-133, 2004) fixed volatile semantics. Go's memory model says a channel send happens before the matching receive completes.

Everyday analogy. Two colleagues each keep a private notebook copy of a shared plan and sync only now and then; without a "sync point" one may act on an old page.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying volatile in C/C++ gives thread safety. It does not (it only stops some compiler optimisations). Use std::atomic.
  • Assuming x86 behaviour proves correctness on ARM.
  • Forgetting that a plain boolean stop flag may never be seen as changed (the JIT can hoist the read out of the loop).

notes.title: Choosing a primitive and finding contention in production
notes.html:
Pick the simplest primitive that is correct, then measure. A decision ladder:

Need Use
Protect a multi-field invariant Mutex
Wait until a condition holds Mutex plus condition variable (or a blocking queue)
Limit N concurrent users of a resource Semaphore
Counter, flag, single pointer swap Atomic
Tiny critical section in a kernel or interrupt Spinlock
Many readers, rare writers Reader-writer lock, or copy-on-write / RCU
Avoid sharing altogether Message passing, thread confinement, per-thread data

Spotting lock contention on a live Linux box:

$ vmstat 1 3
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
12  0      0 812304 120044 2210032    0    0     0     4 9120 118000 38 22 40  0  0

A high cs (context switches, here 118k/s) with CPU idle (id 40) while the app is slow hints at threads parking on locks. Confirm per thread:

pidstat -w -t -p 2310 1      # voluntary context switches per thread
perf trace -s -p 2310 -- sleep 5   # futex dominates the syscall summary
jstack 2310 | grep -A3 "BLOCKED"   # Java: who waits for which monitor

Industry examples. Instagram and Dropbox have both published Python/Go services that stalled on a hot lock around a shared cache; the fix was sharding the lock (hash key to one of 64 locks), the standard first step. Java ConcurrentHashMap does lock striping (bins) by design.

Everyday analogy. Traffic: first remove the shared road (separate lanes), then add a signal (lock) only where roads must cross.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising with lock-free code before measuring contention.
  • Using a read-write lock where writes are frequent: it is slower than a plain mutex because of bookkeeping and writer starvation rules.
  • Not mentioning lock ordering and keeping critical sections short as the first cures.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A race condition is timing-dependent wrongness; counter++ is load, add, store. Detect with ThreadSanitizer or Go -race.
  • Keep critical sections tiny; Amdahl's law says the serial part caps speed-up.
  • Mutex: sleeping lock built on futex (fast path in user space, slow path syscall). Release on all paths; beware priority inversion.
  • Spinlock: busy-wait, only for very short holds, mostly kernel and interrupt context.
  • Semaphore: a counter for N resources or for signalling; no owner.
  • Condition variable: always with a mutex and a while loop; handles spurious and stolen wake-ups.
  • Atomics and CAS: lock-free building blocks; watch ABA, contention and false sharing; shard hot counters.
  • Memory ordering: caches, store buffers and compilers reorder; use release/acquire, volatile (Java) or std::atomic; mutexes already give the fences.
  • In production: high context switches plus idle CPU plus futex in strace points to lock contention.

questions.promptHtml: What is a race condition, and how is it different from a data race? Is counter++ thread-safe?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you can reason about interleavings rather than recite "use a lock", and whether you know the two terms are not synonyms.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A race condition is a bug where correctness depends on the timing of threads. A data race is the narrower, formal case: two threads touch the same memory, at least one writes, and nothing orders them. counter++ is not thread-safe: it is load, add, store, so two threads can both load 5 and both store 6 and one increment is lost. You can also have a race condition with no data race, for example check-balance then withdraw done in two separately locked steps.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
counter++ compiles to three steps. Any interleaving that lets two threads load the same old value loses an update.

Thread A            Thread B            memory
load  r1 = 5                            5
                    load  r2 = 5        5
store 6                                 6
                    store 6             6   <- should be 7

Data race = a property of memory accesses (formal, detectable by tools like ThreadSanitizer). Race condition = a property of program logic (the result depends on ordering). A data race is almost always a race condition; the reverse is not true. Check-then-act (if (balance >= x) balance -= x) with each step individually locked is a race condition without a data race: both threads pass the check, both withdraw.

Why it hides: it fires rarely, and a debugger or a printf changes timing so the bug disappears (Heisenbug). Two threads doing 1M increments each typically end near 1.1 to 1.5M instead of 2M.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: C++, Java, Kotlin, Python

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
#include <atomic>
std::atomic<int> counter{0};
void worker() { for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) counter.fetch_add(1); }
AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
void worker() { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) counter.incrementAndGet(); }
val counter = java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger()
fun worker() { repeat(1_000_000) { counter.incrementAndGet() } }
import threading
lock = threading.Lock()
counter = 0
def worker():
    global counter
    for _ in range(1_000_000):
        with lock:          # counter += 1 is NOT atomic even with the GIL
            counter += 1

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing one line of source is one atomic step.
  • Saying volatile fixes it: volatile gives visibility, not atomic read-modify-write.
  • Using the terms interchangeably; name both and give the check-then-act example.
  • Python: assuming the GIL makes += safe. The GIL can switch between bytecodes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you detect this in CI? -> ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread), Go -race, stress tests with many threads and Thread.sleep jitter.
  2. Give a race condition with no data race. -> Two correctly locked steps (check, then act) that are not atomic together.
  3. Does a lock alone fix check-then-act? -> Only if one lock covers both the check and the act as a single critical section.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "add synchronized". The senior separates the formal data race from the logic race, picks the right fix (atomic, one lock around the whole invariant, or no sharing), and names the tool that finds it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "seats left" or inventory counter that oversells under load is the textbook case; the fix is a conditional atomic update (UPDATE ... WHERE stock > 0) or one lock around check and decrement.

questions.promptHtml: How does a mutex work on Linux, and why is an uncontended lock cheap but a contended one expensive?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat locks as magic from those who know the user-space fast path and the kernel slow path.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On Linux a mutex is a futex: one integer in user memory. Uncontended lock is a single atomic compare-and-swap, around 20 ns, no syscall. If the CAS fails, the thread calls futex(FUTEX_WAIT) and the kernel parks it; unlock sees waiters and calls FUTEX_WAKE. A contended lock therefore costs a syscall plus a context switch, 2 to 10 microseconds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
lock():   CAS(word, 0 -> 1)  success -> done (no kernel)
          fail -> mark word=2 (waiters), futex_wait(word, 2)  -> thread sleeps
unlock(): old = exchange(word, 0); if old == 2 -> futex_wake(word, 1)

The sleeping thread uses no CPU, which is the difference from a spinlock. The wake path costs a scheduler pass and a cold cache on the woken core. A mutex has an owner: only the locker may unlock. Reentrant mutexes (Java synchronized, ReentrantLock) allow the same thread to relock; a default pthread_mutex_t does not, and relocking self-deadlocks.

You see contention in production as futex dominating strace -c, a high context switch rate in vmstat (cs), and idle CPU while latency is bad.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
strace -f -c -p 2310
# % time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
#  91.40    4.812211        1203      4000       812 futex

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to unlock on the exception path. Use RAII (std::lock_guard), try/finally, or defer.
  • Different locks guarding the same data in different code paths.
  • Treating a mutex as free; with many threads it shows up as futex time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the fast path in user space? -> Most locks are uncontended; a syscall (~100s of ns) would dominate.
  2. What is priority inversion? -> Low-priority holder, high-priority waiter, medium thread hogs the CPU; fix with priority inheritance (PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT).
  3. What does Go do against starvation? -> After a waiter fails for 1 ms the mutex switches to starvation mode and hands ownership directly to the oldest waiter.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "a mutex blocks other threads". Senior: describes the futex fast and slow path, the cost numbers, how to see contention with strace and vmstat, and the inversion problem.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Mars Pathfinder kept resetting in 1997 from priority inversion on a mutex; enabling priority inheritance fixed it remotely.

questions.promptHtml: What is a semaphore, and when would you use one instead of a mutex?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know ownership, counting and signalling, not just "a semaphore is a fancy lock".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A semaphore is a counter with wait (decrement, sleep if it would go below zero) and signal (increment, wake a sleeper). It has no owner, so one thread can signal what another waited on. I use a counting semaphore to limit N concurrent users of a resource, such as 20 connections, and a semaphore starting at 0 to signal "event happened". For protecting data I use a mutex, because it has an owner and priority inheritance.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Counting (N permits):   acquire -> permits-- (block at 0)   release -> permits++
Signal (initial 0):     B: wait()  blocks ...   A: signal()  B wakes

Mutex = exclusion + owner. Semaphore = counting + signalling. A binary semaphore used as a mutex has no owner, so a release from the wrong place goes undetected, and there is no priority inheritance. Bulkhead pattern: a semaphore of 25 per app server across 8 servers caps a flaky downstream at 200 concurrent calls; extra callers queue (bounded) or fail fast.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private final Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(10);
String call() throws InterruptedException {
    permits.acquire();
    try { return http.get(url); }
    finally { permits.release(); }   // leak a permit and capacity shrinks forever
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaking permits on exceptions; always release in finally.
  • Using a binary semaphore as a mutex.
  • Not knowing a semaphore can start at 0 to mean "wait for an event".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a semaphore be released by a different thread? -> Yes, that is the point for signalling.
  2. How does a connection pool use one? -> Initial value = pool size; acquire before borrowing.
  3. What happens if release is called more than acquire? -> The count exceeds the intended capacity and the limit silently breaks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The senior explains ownership, picks semaphore for counting/signalling and mutex for data, and mentions the bulkhead pattern and permit leaks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service lost 1 permit per timeout exception (release was not in finally); after a few hours the semaphore hit zero and every request hung.

questions.promptHtml: Why must a condition variable wait sit in a while loop, and what does wait do with the mutex?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The if instead of while bug is the most common real concurrency bug in hand-written queues.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: wait(cv, m) atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then reacquires the mutex before returning. The condition can be false when you wake: spurious wake-ups exist, and another consumer may take the item between the signal and my reacquire. So I always re-check in a while. The condition is changed and signalled under the same mutex that wait uses.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
consumer:                          producer:
  lock(m)                            lock(m)
  while (queue.empty()) wait(cv, m)    queue.push(x)
  x = queue.pop()                      signal(cv)
  unlock(m)                          unlock(m)

Atomic release-and-sleep prevents the lost wake-up window: without atomicity the producer could signal after the consumer checked but before it slept. Signal wakes one waiter; broadcast wakes all (thundering herd) but is needed when waiters wait for different conditions on one cv. glibc uses FUTEX_REQUEUE to move waiters to the mutex queue instead of waking them all.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: C++, Java, Kotlin, Python

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
cv.wait(lk, [&]{ return !q.empty(); });   // predicate form = built-in while loop
auto item = q.front(); q.pop();
lock.lock();
try {
    while (queue.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await();   // loop, not if
    return queue.poll();
} finally { lock.unlock(); }
lock.withLock {
    while (queue.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await()
    return queue.poll()
}
with cond:                       # threading.Condition
    while not queue:
        cond.wait()
    item = queue.popleft()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• if instead of while.
  • Changing the shared state without holding the mutex, causing a lost wake-up.
  • Using a different mutex than the one protecting the state.
  • Signalling before the state change is visible.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Signal vs broadcast? -> Signal wakes one; broadcast when waiters have different predicates or you are unsure; costs a herd.
  2. Why do spurious wake-ups exist? -> Futex/OS implementation freedom; correctness must not depend on them.
  3. What replaces this in practice? -> BlockingQueue, channels; they encapsulate the pattern.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "wait until notified". Senior: explains atomic release-and-sleep, both wake-up failure modes, and defaults to a blocking queue instead of hand-rolling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-written pool using if returned null connections under load, because a stolen wake-up let two threads proceed for one connection.

questions.promptHtml: How does compare-and-swap work, what is the ABA problem, and are atomics always faster than locks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests lock-free fundamentals and whether you know their limits (contention, false sharing).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CAS says "set to new only if the value is still expected, and tell me whether it worked", done by one hardware instruction (lock cmpxchg on x86, LL/SC or LSE on ARM). Lock-free code loops: read, compute, CAS, retry on failure. ABA: the value goes A to B to A, my CAS succeeds although the structure changed; fix with version stamps, hazard pointers or epoch/RCU reclamation. Atomics are not always faster: under heavy contention all cores fight for one cache line, so hot counters should be sharded.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: 8 threads x 10M increments: mutex about 1.5 to 3 s, single atomic about 0.5 to 1 s, sharded counter (per-thread padded slot, sum on read, like LongAdder) about 0.03 s. Atomics remove sleeping, not cache-line bouncing. A CAS loop is lock-free (the system progresses) but not wait-free (one thread can retry forever). Multi-field invariants need a lock; two atomics together are not a consistent pair. False sharing: two unrelated atomics on one 64-byte line slow each other; pad.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: C++, Java, Kotlin, Python

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void record_max(std::atomic<long>& mx, long v) {
    long cur = mx.load();
    while (v > cur && !mx.compare_exchange_weak(cur, v)) {}   // cur refreshed on failure
}
void recordMax(AtomicLong max, long v) {
    long cur;
    while (v > (cur = max.get()) && !max.compareAndSet(cur, v)) { }
}
fun recordMax(max: AtomicLong, v: Long) {
    while (true) {
        val cur = max.get()
        if (v <= cur || max.compareAndSet(cur, v)) return
    }
}
# CPython has no user-level CAS; use a lock or a queue. The GIL does not make
# read-modify-write on a shared int atomic.
with lock:
    if v > mx: mx = v

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Lock-free is always faster."
  • Ignoring false sharing and cache-line bouncing.
  • Treating two atomics as one consistent snapshot.
  • Assuming CAS on pointers is safe against node reuse (ABA).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Lock-free vs wait-free? -> Lock-free: someone always progresses; wait-free: everyone finishes in bounded steps.
  2. How do you fix ABA? -> Stamped reference, hazard pointers, epoch reclamation.
  3. When pick a lock over atomics? -> Multi-field invariants, complex updates, anything you cannot reason about in one CAS.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior gives the sharding numbers, explains why atomics still bounce a line, and names ABA remedies.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A metrics counter incremented on every request became the top CPU line in a profile at 40 cores; switching to LongAdder cut it to noise.

questions.promptHtml: Why can one thread fail to see another thread's write, and what do release/acquire and volatile guarantee?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Visibility bugs only appear on weak-memory hardware or after JIT; it separates people who have read the memory model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Compilers keep values in registers and reorder, and CPUs have store buffers and reorder execution, so another thread may see writes late or in a different order. A release store guarantees all earlier writes are visible to a thread whose acquire load sees that store. Java volatile is acquire on read and release on write; C/C++ volatile is not a thread tool, use std::atomic. A mutex lock is acquire, unlock is release, so data under a mutex needs no extra fences.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
shared: int data = 0; bool ready = false;
A: data = 42; ready = true;          B: while(!ready){}  use(data);   // may see 0

x86 is TSO: only store-then-load to different addresses can reorder. ARM/POWER reorder almost anything, so code that "works on x86" breaks on Android and Apple silicon. Orders in C++: relaxed (atomicity only), acquire, release, acq_rel, seq_cst (default, safest). Double-checked locking was broken before Java 5 because the reference could be published before the constructor finished; declare the field volatile.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: C++, Java, Kotlin, Python

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int data; std::atomic<bool> ready{false};
// A: data = 42; ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);
// B: while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}  use(data);
int data; volatile boolean ready;
// A: data = 42; ready = true;      B: while (!ready) {} use(data);   // sees 42
var data = 0
@Volatile var ready = false
// A: data = 42; ready = true      B: while (!ready) {}; use(data)
# CPython: threading.Event gives the same happens-before edge
ev = threading.Event()
# A: data = 42; ev.set()     B: ev.wait(); use(data)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• C/C++ volatile for threads.
  • Assuming x86 results prove correctness on ARM.
  • A plain boolean stop flag that the JIT hoists out of the loop, so it never sees the change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is happens-before? -> The Java Memory Model relation: a volatile write or unlock happens-before the matching read or lock.
  2. When use relaxed ordering? -> Pure counters/statistics where nothing else depends on the value.
  3. How verify weak-order code? -> ThreadSanitizer, model checkers (CDSChecker, Loom).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows the hardware cause (store buffers, TSO vs weak), uses seq_cst by default, and treats relaxed orders as a measured optimisation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service moved from x86 to ARM instances and a rare stale-config read appeared, because a plain field was published without release semantics.

questions.subtopic: Race condition without a data race
questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service passes TSan cleanly, yet reconciliation shows 0.02% of accounts with negative balances at 3,000 withdrawals/s.

class Wallet {
    private long balance;
    synchronized long get() { return balance; }
    synchronized void set(long v) { balance = v; }
}
void withdraw(Wallet w, long amt) {
    if (w.get() >= amt) {          // check
        w.set(w.get() - amt);      // act
    }
}

Red herring: the team already "made everything synchronized" last quarter.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why TSan is silent, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add volatile" or "synchronize withdraw too much" without seeing that each call is individually atomic but the sequence is not.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Wallet shared by many request threads (yes, per account)? Is there a DB behind it that is the real source of truth? What invariant must hold (balance >= 0)? Any multi-instance deployment (a JVM lock will not help there)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a DB-level CHECK (balance >= 0) or a conditional update so negative balances cannot persist, and run a reconciliation job.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) check-then-act across two synchronized calls; (b) a second app instance writing the same account; (c) lost update in the read-modify-write via get/set; (d) overflow (unlikely at these numbers).
  4. How I'd verify each: Write a stress test with 16 threads withdrawing 1 from a balance of 1000 and assert the final balance; log thread ids around the negative cases; check deployment count.
  5. Root cause: Two threads both pass get() >= amt, then both set(get() - amt). Every access is synchronized, so there is no data race and TSan is silent; it is a race condition because the invariant spans several calls.
  6. Fix: Short-term: make the whole operation one critical section.
synchronized boolean withdraw(long amt) {
    if (balance < amt) return false;
    balance -= amt; return true;
}

Long-term: if more than one instance exists, do it in the database: UPDATE wallet SET bal = bal - ? WHERE id = ? AND bal >= ? and check the row count. 7. Prevention: Expose operations that enforce invariants, not raw get/set; a jcstress or stress test in CI; review rule: no if (x.get()) x.set(). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make balance volatile or wrap get in more locks; that adds cost without ordering the two steps. One lock per wallet is fine at 3,000/s; a global lock would serialise unrelated accounts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if two JVMs serve the same wallet? -> The in-process lock is useless; use the conditional SQL update or optimistic versioning.
  • Why not AtomicLong? -> compareAndSet in a loop works for a single field and is fine here; a lock is simpler if a history must update together.
  • Would a stricter TSan config find it? -> No, there is no data race to find; you need invariant-based tests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A ticketing team "fixed" overselling by marking getters synchronized; oversell dropped from 5% to 0.1% and everyone thought it solved. The remaining 0.1% was this exact two-call pattern, found only by a randomized stress test with an invariant assert.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests volatile, or says "TSan is wrong".
  • Hire: finds check-then-act, merges into one synchronized method.
  • Strong hire: distinguishes data race from race condition, covers multi-instance and DB conditional update, adds invariant stress test.

questions.contextHtml:
A hand-rolled job queue in C++ occasionally hangs: one worker sleeps forever while jobs sit in the queue. Happens about once per 50 million jobs, never in unit tests.

std::mutex m; std::condition_variable cv; std::queue<Job> q; bool done = false;

void push(Job j) {
    { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m); q.push(j); }
    cv.notify_one();
}
Job pop() {
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
    if (q.empty()) cv.wait(lk);        // line A
    Job j = q.front(); q.pop();        // sometimes crashes: pop on empty
    return j;
}

With 8 workers, top shows low CPU and strace -f shows several threads in futex_wait.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both failure modes and give a corrected version including shutdown.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably a deadlock, add a timeout to wait." Papers over the bug and keeps the crash.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: One producer or many? Can push race with shutdown? Compiler and libstdc++ version? Is there a core file from the pop-on-empty crash?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart workers with a watchdog that dumps stacks; capture a core to confirm.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) if instead of while: stolen or spurious wake-up makes a worker pop an empty queue (the crash); (b) lost wake-up around shutdown, as done is never checked in the wait; (c) a stale notify_one waking a worker that cannot make progress while another sleeps; (d) memory corruption (least likely).
  4. How I'd verify each: gdb -p PID -batch -ex "thread apply all bt" to see where threads sleep; a stress test with 1 producer, 16 consumers, random sleeps; helgrind/TSan on the test.
  5. Root cause: if instead of while. Between notify_one and the woken thread reacquiring m, another worker may take the item; the woken thread proceeds on an empty queue. Separately there is no done predicate, so shutdown leaves sleepers waiting forever.
  6. Fix: Short-term: predicate wait.
Job pop(bool& ok) {
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
    cv.wait(lk, [&]{ return !q.empty() || done; });
    if (q.empty()) { ok = false; return {}; }   // shut down and drained
    Job j = q.front(); q.pop(); ok = true; return j;
}
void shutdown() { { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m); done = true; } cv.notify_all(); }

Long-term: replace with a tested blocking queue. 7. Prevention: Lint rule/clang-tidy for cv.wait without predicate; stress test with TSan in CI; shutdown test. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use wait_for timeouts as a fix: hides the bug and adds latency. notify_all on every push is safe but a thundering herd; keep notify_one since each push adds one item.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is notifying outside the lock a bug? -> No, the state change was under the lock; it is fine and often faster.
  • Why only once per 50M jobs? -> The window between notify and reacquire is nanoseconds; needs an exact interleaving.
  • Would a semaphore be simpler? -> Yes for counting items, but shutdown signalling still needs thought.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue "worked for a year" until a faster CPU narrowed the timing window differently and a nightly batch started crashing. The fix was one word, if to while, after three days of core files.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests timeouts or "more locking".
  • Hire: converts to while/predicate and adds shutdown flag.
  • Strong hire: explains stolen vs spurious wake-up, uses TSan/stress to prove, replaces with a library queue.

questions.contextHtml: A request handler takes about 255 microseconds: 50 us parsing, 5 us updating a shared stats map, 200 us writing the response. A refactor wrapped the whole handler body in the stats mutex "for safety". The service on a 32-core box now peaks at 4,900 req/s and CPU sits at 12%, whereas before it hit 120,000 req/s. strace -c shows futex at 88% of syscall time.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the numbers and what you change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use more threads" or "switch to a faster lock". Neither shrinks the serial fraction.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 255 us breakdown measured or guessed? Is the map read as well as written? Is exact consistency of stats required per request? Can I see the diff of the refactor?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the refactor, or narrow the lock to the 5 us update.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lock held across the response write (serial 255 us); (b) lock held across I/O; (c) too many threads convoying; (d) GC pause (red herring: CPU is low, not spiking).
  4. How I'd verify each: Throughput bound = 1 / 255 us = about 3,900 to 4,900 req/s, which matches. perf or a lock profiler (jstack sample, async-profiler lock mode) to see time in the monitor.
  5. Root cause: Amdahl: with the whole handler serial, speed-up cap is about 1x; with only 5 of 255 us serial it is 255/5 = 51x, so 32 cores are usable. Threads sleep in futex so CPU is idle.
  6. Fix: Short-term: lock only the update.
Stats local = parseAndBuild(req);          // parallel
synchronized (statsLock) { stats.merge(local); }   // ~5 us
writeResponse(resp);                        // parallel

Long-term: per-thread stats merged periodically, or LongAdder/sharded map, removing the lock from the hot path. 7. Prevention: Code review rule: no I/O or callbacks under a lock; a load test gate on throughput; lock-hold-time metric. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not go lock-free first; shrinking the section gives 25x and costs nothing. Per-thread stats cost a little staleness and memory.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the stats update itself becomes 50 us? -> Cap is 255/50 = 5x; shard or batch.
  • Is "safe" wrong? -> Correct but coarse; correctness only needs the shared state protected.
  • Should reads of stats take the lock? -> If writers exist, yes or use immutable snapshots.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team scaled a service from 8 to 64 cores and saw nothing; a single logging call inside a lock was 90% of the serial time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the machine or adds threads.
  • Hire: moves I/O out of the lock, gives Amdahl reasoning.
  • Strong hire: computes the bound, reproduces numbers, proposes sharding and a hold-time metric.

questions.contextHtml:
A C++ in-memory cache uses a home-grown test-and-set spinlock (while(flag.exchange(1)) {}) around a hash lookup (~100 ns). It ran fine on 8-core VMs. After moving to Kubernetes with 4-CPU limits on a 64-core host and a pool of 32 worker threads, p99 went from 2 ms to 600 ms and CPU is pegged at 400%.

$ perf top
 71.3%  cache  [.] SpinLock::lock
$ pidstat -w -t 1     (per thread)
 nvcswch/s  low   ... nivcswch/s 2400   <- involuntary context switches high

Throttling shows in cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat: nr_throttled growing fast. The lock is held for ~100 ns.
questions.promptHtml: Why did a 100 ns lock become a disaster, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Spinlocks are fast, so it must be the network" or "just add more CPU". Misses the preempted-holder problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many runnable threads vs CPU limit? Is the container CFS-quota throttled? What is the lock hold time distribution including page faults? Do reads and writes both take it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cut worker threads to the CPU limit (4) or raise the CPU limit; if possible swap in std::mutex.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) oversubscription: 32 threads on 4 CPUs, the lock holder gets preempted and others spin the whole quantum (~4 ms); (b) cgroup throttling freezes a holder for up to the rest of the 100 ms period; (c) cache-line stampede from test-and-set; (d) slow hash (red herring: 100 ns is measured).
  4. How I'd verify each: perf top (spin symbol), pidstat -w -t (involuntary switches), cpu.stat for throttle counts, thread count vs nproc in the container.
  5. Root cause: A spinlock assumes the holder keeps running. With more threads than CPUs, or when CFS throttles the cgroup, the holder is descheduled with the lock held and every other runnable thread burns its time slice spinning. A 100 ns hold becomes a multi-millisecond stall.
  6. Fix: Short-term: size the pool to the CPU quota. Long-term: use an adaptive mutex (spin a few iterations then futex-sleep), shard the cache by key hash across 64 locks, or use read-mostly structures.
// shard the lock: each shard has its own mutex
auto& s = shards[std::hash<K>{}(key) % 64];
std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(s.m);
  1. Prevention: Load test at container limits, not on bare metal; alert on nr_throttled; ban raw spinlocks in user space unless pinned and measured.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add sched_yield in the spin loop as a patch (unpredictable, still wastes CPU). Mutex costs ~5 us on contention but never collapses.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would pinning threads to cores help? -> Yes for the oversubscription case, but throttling remains with CFS quotas.
  • Why does the kernel get away with spinlocks? -> It disables preemption while holding them, so the holder cannot be descheduled.
  • What about a ticket lock? -> Fair, but a preempted ticket holder or waiter is even worse (queue convoy).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A pricing service tuned on dedicated hosts collapsed after moving to containers; the lock hold stayed 100 ns while the effective stall became 10 ms per preemption.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the hash or blames the network.
  • Hire: identifies spin plus oversubscription, switches to mutex.
  • Strong hire: ties throttling and preemption to a lock holder, shards locks, adds throttle alerts.

questions.contextHtml:
A Java order service doubled traffic after a promotion. p99 goes 80 ms to 1.4 s, error rate is flat, CPU 38%, memory fine. Heap GC logs show pauses under 20 ms.

$ vmstat 1 3
 r  b   swpd   free   cache  ...   in    cs us sy id wa
14  0      0 812304 2210032  ... 9120 118000 21 17 62  0
$ perf trace -s -p 2310 -- sleep 5   (summary)
 futex  calls 410,220  total 38,900 ms
$ jstack 2310 | grep -c BLOCKED
147

The latest release added a shared Map<String, Rate> guarded by one synchronized method for currency conversion.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix, then say how you would pick the final design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale out the pods." That multiplies the lock count and does not fix the serial section; also blames GC with no evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which release changed things and when did p99 start moving? Is the rate map read-heavy? How long is the critical section? Are there multiple JVMs? Is latency uniform or only in some endpoints?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the release or add pods temporarily to buy time; take 3 thread dumps 5 s apart first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lock contention on the map's monitor (high cs, 62% idle, futex, 147 BLOCKED); (b) GC (ruled out: pauses 20 ms); (c) DB or downstream slowness (check span timings); (d) thread pool exhaustion as a symptom of (a).
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack x3: same monitor 0x... with one owner and many waiters; async-profiler -e lock; JFR monitor-blocked events; compare against a heap/GC log.
  5. Root cause: One monitor serialises every request; hold time x arrival rate saturates it. Once utilisation of the lock nears 100%, waiting time explodes non-linearly (queueing), which is why doubling traffic gave 17x latency.
  6. Fix: Short-term: copy-on-write snapshot, because rates change a few times an hour.
private volatile Map<String, Rate> rates = Map.of();
Rate get(String c) { return rates.get(c); }                  // no lock
void refresh(Map<String, Rate> fresh) { rates = Map.copyOf(fresh); }

Long-term: ConcurrentHashMap if updates are frequent; keep lock hold times in a dashboard. 7. Prevention: Load test before release at 2x peak; metric for lock wait (JFR/async-profiler in staging); review check "shared mutable map behind a global lock". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not jump to lock-free structures or a read-write lock; a read-mostly map is simplest as an immutable snapshot. Staleness of seconds is acceptable for rates (confirm with product).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if rates update 1000 times a second? -> ConcurrentHashMap (striped), or sharded locks.
  • Why is CPU only 38%? -> Threads sleep on the monitor; idle CPU with high latency is the contention fingerprint.
  • Would more heap help? -> No; GC is not the bottleneck.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "harmless" static synchronized helper was called from every request path; one flame graph in lock mode showed 70% of wall time waiting on it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales out or tunes GC.
  • Hire: spots futex plus BLOCKED plus idle CPU, replaces the lock.
  • Strong hire: explains queueing non-linearity, uses lock profiling tools, chooses snapshot with staleness reasoning.

questions.contextHtml:
A metrics library increments one AtomicLong requests on every request. At 20k req/s on 8 cores it was invisible. The service is being scaled to 200k req/s on 64-core machines. A perf profile at the new load shows:

 18.2%  libmetrics  Counter::inc    (lock xadd)
  9.1%  app         Handler::serve
 L1d cache misses: 31% of loads on cores that touch the counter

Adjacent in the same object are AtomicLong errors and AtomicLong bytes, each updated by different request paths.
questions.promptHtml: Why does a lock-free increment cost 18% of CPU, and how do you fix it without losing accuracy?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Atomics are lock-free so they scale". Ignores that all cores contend for one cache line.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the value read per request or only on scrape? Do we need an exact real-time value? Is the counter object laid out contiguously? What is the scrape interval?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Increment by batches per thread (every 100 requests) or sample 1 in 10 for non-critical counters.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) cache-line bouncing on one hot line across 64 cores; (b) false sharing between requests, errors, bytes on the same 64-byte line; (c) NUMA cross-socket traffic; (d) contention in an unrelated lock (red herring: profile shows lock xadd).
  4. How I'd verify each: perf c2c for false sharing, perf stat -e cache-misses, a microbenchmark with 1, 8, 64 threads; check object layout.
  5. Root cause: Every lock xadd needs exclusive ownership of the line; with 64 writers the line migrates between cores constantly (about 50 to 100 ns per transfer). Throughput per counter is capped no matter how many cores exist.
  6. Fix: Shard: each thread (or CPU slot) updates its own padded cell; sum on read.
LongAdder requests = new LongAdder();
requests.increment();            // contended cells spread automatically
long total = requests.sum();     // read on scrape; not a snapshot, fine for metrics

In C++ use per-thread alignas(64) counters aggregated by the scraper. 7. Prevention: Microbenchmark hot-path metrics at 64 threads; @Contended/padding conventions; benchmarks in CI. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: sum() is not an atomic snapshot and costs O(cells); do not use it for control decisions such as rate limits that need an exact value. I would not remove metrics.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does LongAdder suit a "reserve 1 if below limit" counter? -> No, it cannot make atomic decisions; use a single atomic or a token-bucket per shard.
  • What is false sharing? -> Different variables on one line invalidating each other's cache.
  • Does it help on ARM? -> Yes; weak memory makes bouncing no cheaper.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team found 15% of their API's CPU was one request counter; sharding it paid for the next hardware refresh.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "atomics are free".
  • Hire: knows cache-line contention and uses LongAdder or sharding.
  • Strong hire: also finds false sharing with perf c2c, discusses read semantics and when sharding is wrong.

questions.contextHtml:
You are migrating a Java and C++ pricing service from x86 to ARM (Graviton-class) instances, 10% canary. After one hour, 3 of 40 canary pods publish stale prices, about one in 10 million reads, and one pod never stops on shutdown. Unit and integration tests pass. The code:

class PriceBook {
    private Map<String, Price> book = new HashMap<>();
    private boolean stop;                       // read in worker loop
    void publish(Map<String, Price> fresh) { book = fresh; }   // called from refresher
    Price get(String k) { return book.get(k); }
    void run() { while (!stop) { work(); } }
    void shutdown() { stop = true; }
}
static Foo inst;
static Foo get() { if (inst == null) { synchronized (X.class) { if (inst == null) inst = new Foo(); } } return inst; }
questions.promptHtml: Why did this surface only on ARM, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably an ARM bug in the JVM." The code is wrong on every platform; x86's strong ordering hid it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: JVM version and flags? Does the refresher run on a different thread than readers (yes)? Is Price immutable? Do the stale reads include partially built objects?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the canary rollout; stay on x86 for the pricing fleet until fixed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) unsafe publication of book and inst; (b) non-volatile stop hoisted by the JIT (the stuck shutdown); (c) HashMap built then published without a happens-before edge; (d) GC or clock skew (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: jcstress tests for the publication pattern; run the code on ARM with stress; review for a final/volatile on each cross-thread field; JIT flags such as -XX:+PrintCompilation only if needed.
  5. Root cause: No happens-before between the writer thread and readers. On x86 (TSO) stores become visible in order, hiding the bug. ARM can reorder the stores that fill the map with the store that publishes the reference, and the JIT may keep stop in a register.
  6. Fix: Short-term: volatile on book, stop, and inst, and make Price and the map immutable (Map.copyOf).
private volatile Map<String, Price> book = Map.of();
private volatile boolean stop;
private static volatile Foo inst;     // fixes double-checked locking

Long-term: use the holder idiom or an enum singleton; prefer message passing/atomic snapshots. 7. Prevention: Run concurrency tests on ARM in CI; jcstress; TSan for the C++ half; review rule: every cross-thread field is final, volatile, atomic, or guarded. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not sprinkle synchronized everywhere, nor rely on "it works on x86". volatile read cost on ARM is small (an ldar).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is double-checked locking broken without volatile? -> Reference can be published before the constructor's writes are visible.
  • Is HashMap read-only after publication safe? -> Yes, if published through a volatile/final edge and never mutated again.
  • Same issue in C++? -> Use std::atomic<T*> with release/acquire; plain bool is a data race (UB).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's flaky "stuck shutdown" was dismissed for a year; ARM hardware made it reproducible in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the JVM or hardware.
  • Hire: names missing happens-before and adds volatile.
  • Strong hire: explains TSO vs weak ordering, JIT hoisting, immutable snapshots, ARM CI and jcstress.

questions.contextHtml:
A soft real-time telemetry gateway on Linux runs a control thread (SCHED_FIFO priority 80), a logging thread (nice 0), and 6 medium-priority (SCHED_FIFO 50) compression threads. Once or twice a day the control loop misses its 5 ms deadline by 300 to 900 ms and the watchdog resets the unit.

perf sched latency:  control_loop  max delay 812 ms
stack of control_loop (cat /proc/PID/stack):  futex_wait_queue -> ... pthread_mutex_lock (log_mutex)
logger thread state: runnable, not running (preempted by compress-*)

log_mutex protects a shared ring buffer that both the logger and control thread write to; hold time is 10 us.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure and fix it without rewriting the architecture.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The mutex is slow, use a spinlock". Spinning makes it worse: the high-priority thread would burn CPU waiting for a thread that cannot run.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which threads take log_mutex? Is the mutex created with priority inheritance? What is the kernel (PREEMPT_RT?) and are the compress threads CPU bound?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin compress threads to other cores or lower their priority below the logger; stop the control thread logging in the hot path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) priority inversion: low logger holds the mutex, high control thread waits, medium compress threads preempt the logger; (b) I/O stall inside the critical section; (c) scheduler throttling (sched_rt_runtime_us); (d) interrupt storm (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: perf sched, trace-cmd/ftrace sched_switch around the miss, check pthread_mutexattr_getprotocol, cat /proc/sys/kernel/sched_rt_runtime_us.
  5. Root cause: The logger (low) is preempted while holding the mutex; the control thread (high) waits for it; the 6 medium threads keep the CPU so the logger never runs to release: high priority waits on the medium ones. This is the Mars Pathfinder failure.
  6. Fix: Short-term: initialise the mutex with priority inheritance.
pthread_mutexattr_t a; pthread_mutexattr_init(&a);
pthread_mutexattr_setprotocol(&a, PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT);
pthread_mutex_init(&log_mutex, &a);

Long-term: remove sharing, give the control thread a lock-free single-producer ring buffer that the logger drains. 7. Prevention: Priority-aware design review; latency tests with CPU-hog threads; max-latency alerts using cyclictest. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not bump the logger to priority 80 permanently (starves others). PI mutexes cost slightly more per operation; acceptable for a 10 us section.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does priority inheritance fix a spinlock? -> No, there is no kernel-visible wait.
  • What is priority ceiling? -> Lock gets the highest priority of any user, avoiding chains; more rigid.
  • Does it matter on normal CFS servers? -> Rarely, but it shows up with RT classes and nice levels under saturation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A device vendor spent weeks blaming the radio driver for random resets; ftrace showed a logging mutex was the culprit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests spinlock or "make it faster".
  • Hire: names priority inversion and enables PI.
  • Strong hire: proves it with sched traces, redesigns to a lock-free ring, notes ceiling vs inheritance trade-offs.
